clinicalPearls: Heartburn or chest pain triggered by reflux events despite physiologically normal oesophageal acid exposure
It is distinguished from functional heartburn by a positive association between symptoms and reflux episodes on monitoring
It is distinguished from reflux disease by the absence of excessive acid exposure and of mucosal injury
Both acidic and weakly acidic reflux events can trigger symptoms in sensitised patients
Diagnosis rests on endoscopy plus ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring with symptom-association analysis
Treatment may combine acid suppression or reflux-reducing measures with neuromodulators targeting hypersensitivity
reference.pathophysiology: Reflux hypersensitivity is a disorder of gut-brain interaction in which the oesophagus perceives physiological reflux as painful. Although total acid exposure is within normal limits and the mucosa is intact, peripheral and central sensitisation lowers the threshold at which reflux events, whether acidic or weakly acidic, provoke symptoms. The positive temporal correlation between reflux episodes and symptoms defines the condition and separates it from functional heartburn, in which no such correlation exists.
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsies to exclude mucosal and eosinophilic disease
Ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring showing normal acid exposure but positive symptom association
Oesophageal manometry to exclude a motility disorder
Assessment of response to prior acid suppression
redFlags: Alarm features such as dysphagia, weight loss or bleeding
Objective testing not supporting the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign, and symptom control is often achievable by reducing reflux events and using neuromodulators to lower hypersensitivity.
pitfalls: Confusing it with functional heartburn (which lacks symptom-reflux correlation)
Assuming reflux disease and escalating acid suppression alone
Omitting symptom-association analysis on reflux monitoring
Missing eosinophilic oesophagitis or cardiac chest pain
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Reduce reflux events with a trial of proton pump inhibitor acid suppression and reflux-reducing lifestyle measures such as weight loss, avoiding late meals and elevating the head of the bed
Use neuromodulators such as low-dose tricyclic antidepressants or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors to target oesophageal hypersensitivity
Confirm the diagnosis with endoscopy and pH-impedance monitoring showing normal acid exposure but positive symptom association
Address psychological contributors with reassurance and psychological therapies where relevant
Consider anti-reflux surgery in carefully selected patients with a genuine, well-documented reflux trigger
Refer to gastroenterology for symptoms refractory to combined acid-suppressing and neuromodulatory treatment
